lessonPlan.title: Diodes and rectifiers
lessonPlan.governingQuestion: How does a diode-based power supply turn AC from the wall into steady DC, and how do we analyse each stage?
lessonPlan.canDo: Explain, calculate and design each stage of a simple AC-to-DC power supply, and write it in exam-ready English.

mece.dimension: Stage of the AC-to-DC power-supply chain: the device, then rectify, filter, regulate
mece.rationale: Each stage changes the signal in exactly one way: the diode switches, the rectifier makes it one-directional, the filter smooths it, the regulator holds it constant. A linear power supply is exactly these four stages, so every chapter topic belongs to one stage and no stage is missing.
outOfScope: LEDs, photodiodes and other special diodes beyond the Zener

syllabusLines.text: PN junction diode: formation of the depletion region, barrier potential
Forward and reverse bias; V-I characteristics
Half-wave and full-wave rectifiers (centre-tap and bridge)
Ripple factor, rectification efficiency, peak inverse voltage
Zener diode; Zener diode as a voltage regulator

broadConcepts.title: The PN junction diode
broadConcepts.governingQuestion: What is a diode, how does it behave, and how do we model it in a circuit?

mece.dimension: Level of description of the diode: physical structure, bias behaviour, measured characteristic, circuit model
mece.rationale: Each level answers a different question (why, what happens, what we measure, how we calculate) and together they are everything the later stages need from the diode.
outOfScope: Band diagrams and carrier transport equations

broadConcepts.title: Rectification: AC to pulsating DC
broadConcepts.governingQuestion: How do diode circuits make current flow in one direction, and how do we compare them?

mece.dimension: What a student must know about rectifiers: each circuit's working (three topologies), then the shared measures that compare them
mece.rationale: The three circuits don't overlap: one diode, two diodes with a centre tap, four diodes in a bridge. The figures of merit are taught once in their own concept instead of being repeated inside each circuit, which keeps the circuit concepts exclusive.

broadConcepts.title: Filtering: pulsating DC to smooth DC
broadConcepts.governingQuestion: How does a capacitor smooth rectified DC, and how big must it be?

mece.dimension: Qualitative versus quantitative: how the filter works, then how much ripple it leaves
mece.rationale: The first concept builds the picture, the second turns it into numbers for design; nothing about the capacitor filter falls outside these two.

broadConcepts.title: Regulation: smooth DC to constant DC
broadConcepts.governingQuestion: How does a Zener diode hold the output voltage constant?

mece.dimension: The device versus the circuit that uses it
mece.rationale: First the Zener diode on its own (breakdown and its characteristic), then the regulator built from it; the two don't overlap and together cover the topic.
outOfScope: IC voltage regulators such as the 78xx series

concepts.title: PN junction and the depletion region
concepts.canDo: Explain how a depletion region forms when p-type and n-type silicon meet.

misconceptions.statement: The depletion region is full of free electrons.
misconceptions.correction: It has almost no free carriers; only fixed ions remain.

misconceptions.statement: The barrier potential can be measured with a voltmeter across the diode.
misconceptions.correction: It is internal; the contact potentials at the terminals cancel it out.

explanation.keyIdea: Carriers cross the junction and recombine, leaving fixed ions whose field builds a barrier of about 0.7 V in silicon.
explanation.text: A PN junction forms where p-type silicon (majority carriers: holes) meets n-type silicon (majority carriers: electrons). Electrons diffuse from the n-side into the p-side and recombine with holes, and holes diffuse the other way. This leaves a thin layer near the junction with no free carriers, only fixed ions: negative ions on the p-side and positive ions on the n-side. This layer is the depletion region. The fixed ions create an electric field that opposes further diffusion, so a barrier potential builds up, about 0.7 V for silicon and 0.3 V for germanium. At equilibrium, diffusion stops.

visual.description: A bar split into p (left, holes as small circles) and n (right, electrons as dots). A shaded middle strip labelled 'depletion region' with minus signs on the p-side and plus signs on the n-side, a field arrow from n to p, and a small potential-hill graph below marked 0.7 V.
visual.alt: PN junction with the depletion region, fixed ions, electric field and a 0.7 V barrier

walkthrough.say: A PN junction is where p-type and n-type silicon meet.
Carriers recombine near the junction and leave only fixed ions: the depletion region.
The field of those ions opposes further diffusion, so the junction settles.
That field is the barrier potential: about 0.7 V in silicon.

beats: Holes and electrons drift towards the junction
They meet and vanish in pairs near the junction
Fixed ions remain and a field arrow grows
Diffusion stops: the depletion region has formed

example.title: Two crowded rooms with an open door
example.scenario: Open a door between a room of people (holes) and a room of different people (electrons). People cross and pair off near the door, leaving an empty strip guarded by people who cannot move. Soon the guards stop anyone else from crossing.
example.takeaway: The empty strip is the depletion region, and the guards' push-back is the barrier potential.

workedQuestion.prompt: Explain the formation of the depletion region in a PN junction with a neat diagram.
modelAnswer: A PN junction is formed when a p-type semiconductor is joined to an n-type semiconductor.
In the p-type region holes are the majority carriers; in the n-type region electrons are the majority carriers.
Because of the concentration difference, electrons diffuse from the n-side to the p-side and holes diffuse from the p-side to the n-side, where they recombine.

Recombination leaves immobile negative acceptor ions on the p-side and immobile positive donor ions on the n-side near the junction. This region, with no free charge carriers, is called the depletion region.

These ions set up an electric field from the n-side to the p-side that opposes further diffusion. The resulting potential difference is the barrier potential: about 0.7 V for silicon and 0.3 V for germanium.
(Diagram: p and n regions, the depletion region with − and + ions, the field arrow and the barrier potential.)

rubric.criterion: Defines the PN junction and names the majority carriers
Explains the immobile ions and names the depletion region
Explains the field and the barrier potential with values

checks.prompt: The depletion region mainly contains:
options: Equal numbers of free electrons and holes
checks.answer: Immobile ions
checks.explanation: Free carriers recombine near the junction; only the fixed ions remain.

checks.prompt: Match the term: barrier potential
options: The voltage across the depletion region that opposes diffusion
checks.answer: The voltage across the depletion region that opposes diffusion
checks.explanation: It is an internal voltage set up by the fixed ions.

checks.prompt: The barrier potential of a silicon junction at room temperature is about:
checks.explanation: Silicon: about 0.7 V. Germanium: about 0.3 V.

checks.prompt: In one sentence, explain why diffusion stops at a PN junction.
checks.answer: The electric field of the immobile ions in the depletion region opposes further diffusion of carriers.
checks.explanation: Key words to use: electric field, immobile ions, opposes, diffusion.

concepts.title: Forward and reverse bias
concepts.canDo: Explain why a diode conducts in forward bias and blocks in reverse bias.

misconceptions.statement: Reverse current is exactly zero.
misconceptions.correction: A tiny reverse saturation current of minority carriers flows.

misconceptions.statement: Any forward voltage makes a diode conduct strongly.
misconceptions.correction: A silicon diode conducts strongly only above about 0.7 V.

misconceptions.statement: It doesn't matter which way round the diode is connected.
misconceptions.correction: The orientation decides whether it is forward or reverse biased.

explanation.keyIdea: Forward bias narrows the depletion region so the diode conducts; reverse bias widens it so the diode blocks.
explanation.text: Biasing means applying an external voltage to the diode. In forward bias, the p-side is connected to the positive terminal. This pushes carriers towards the junction, narrows the depletion region and lowers the barrier, so once the applied voltage is above about 0.7 V the diode conducts a large current. In reverse bias, the p-side is connected to the negative terminal. Carriers are pulled away from the junction, the depletion region widens and the barrier rises, so the diode blocks current. Only a tiny reverse saturation current of minority carriers flows, in nanoamperes for silicon.

visual.description: Two circuits side by side. Left: battery positive to the p-side, a narrow depletion strip, a current arrow and a lit bulb. Right: battery negative to the p-side, a wide depletion strip, no current, bulb off.
visual.alt: Forward-biased diode lighting a bulb next to a reverse-biased diode with the bulb off

walkthrough.say: In forward bias, the p-side goes to the positive terminal.
That narrows the depletion region and lowers the barrier.
Exam word: the diode conducts. Don't write that it passes current.
In reverse bias the depletion region widens, so the diode blocks current.

beats: Forward bias: battery positive to p
The depletion region narrows and current flows
Reverse bias: battery negative to p
The depletion region widens and current is blocked

example.title: Reverse-polarity protection
example.scenario: A diode in series with a toy's battery holder lets current flow when the cells go in the right way round. If someone puts them in backwards, the diode is reverse biased and blocks current, so the circuit isn't damaged.
example.takeaway: Forward bias conducts, reverse bias blocks: the diode is a one-way gate.

workedQuestion.prompt: Compare forward bias and reverse bias of a PN junction diode.
modelAnswer: Connection: in forward bias the p-side is connected to the positive terminal; in reverse bias the p-side is connected to the negative terminal.
Depletion region: it narrows in forward bias and widens in reverse bias.
Barrier potential: it decreases in forward bias and increases in reverse bias.
Current: a large forward current (milliamperes) flows once the voltage exceeds about 0.7 V; in reverse bias only a very small reverse saturation current (nanoamperes) flows.
Resistance: the diode's resistance is low in forward bias and very high in reverse bias.

rubric.criterion: Current in each bias, with magnitudes

checks.prompt: In reverse bias, the depletion region:
checks.answer: Widens
checks.explanation: Carriers are pulled away from the junction, so the depletion region widens.

checks.prompt: Match the term: forward bias
options: The p-side connected to the positive terminal
The n-side connected to the positive terminal
checks.answer: The p-side connected to the positive terminal
checks.explanation: Positive to p is forward bias.

checks.prompt: Why does a reverse-biased diode not conduct?
checks.answer: In reverse bias the depletion region widens and the barrier rises, so majority carriers cannot cross and the diode blocks current.
checks.explanation: Concept: wider depletion region. English: use 'widens' and 'blocks'.

checks.prompt: Say in English: when does a diode conduct?
checks.answer: A diode conducts when it is forward biased and the applied voltage is above the cut-in voltage.
checks.explanation: Use 'conducts' and 'forward biased'.

concepts.title: V-I characteristic and cut-in voltage
concepts.canDo: Draw the V-I characteristic of a silicon diode and explain each region.

misconceptions.statement: Diode current rises in a straight line with voltage, like a resistor.
misconceptions.correction: It is exponential: almost nothing, then a steep rise after the cut-in voltage.

misconceptions.statement: Breakdown always destroys a diode.
misconceptions.correction: It can destroy an ordinary diode, but a Zener diode is designed to work there.

explanation.keyIdea: Almost no current until about 0.7 V, then a steep rise; in reverse, a tiny current until breakdown.
explanation.text: The V-I characteristic is the graph of diode current against the voltage across it. In forward bias, the current stays almost zero until the voltage reaches the cut-in voltage, about 0.7 V for silicon, and then rises steeply, almost exponentially. In reverse bias, a very small, nearly constant reverse saturation current flows. If the reverse voltage reaches the breakdown voltage, the current rises sharply, which can destroy an ordinary diode. The curve follows the diode equation I = Is(e^(V/ηVT) − 1).

visual.description: V-I curve: forward branch flat until 0.7 V then steep; reverse branch with a tiny constant current, then a sharp drop at breakdown. Labels: cut-in voltage, reverse saturation current, breakdown voltage.
visual.alt: Silicon diode V-I characteristic with cut-in voltage, reverse saturation current and breakdown marked

walkthrough.say: The V-I characteristic is the graph of current against voltage.
The cut-in voltage is about 0.7 V for silicon.
After the cut-in voltage, current rises steeply. See the knee on the graph.
At the breakdown voltage, reverse current shoots up.

beats: Plot current against voltage
Forward: flat, then the knee at 0.7 V
Reverse: a tiny saturation current
Breakdown: the sharp drop

interactive.prompt: Drag the forward voltage and watch the current. Where does it start to rise?

example.title: Measuring a 1N4007 in the lab
example.scenario: Sweeping the voltage across a 1N4007 silicon diode, the current is almost 0 mA at 0.5 V, a few milliamperes near 0.7 V and tens of milliamperes by 0.8 V.
example.takeaway: That steep knee is why we treat a conducting silicon diode as having about 0.7 V across it.

workedQuestion.prompt: Draw the V-I characteristic of a silicon diode. Mark the cut-in voltage, reverse saturation current and breakdown voltage, and explain each region.
modelAnswer: (Graph: forward current on the positive y-axis, reverse current on the negative y-axis, voltage on the x-axis.)
Forward region: the current is nearly zero until the cut-in voltage (about 0.7 V for silicon); beyond it, the current increases rapidly.
Reverse region: a very small reverse saturation current flows, almost independent of the reverse voltage.
Breakdown region: at the breakdown voltage the reverse current increases sharply; an ordinary diode can be damaged here.
The curve follows the diode equation I = Is(e^(V/ηVT) − 1), where Is is the reverse saturation current and VT ≈ 26 mV at room temperature.

checks.prompt: On the V-I curve of a silicon diode, the forward current at 0.3 V is:
checks.answer: Almost zero
checks.explanation: 0.3 V is below the 0.7 V cut-in voltage.

checks.prompt: Match the term: cut-in voltage
options: The forward voltage above which current rises sharply
The reverse voltage at which current shoots up
checks.answer: The forward voltage above which current rises sharply
checks.explanation: The second option describes the breakdown voltage.

checks.prompt: Sketch the forward part of the V-I curve and mark the cut-in voltage.
checks.answer: Flat near zero up to about 0.7 V, then a steep rise; 0.7 V marked at the knee.
checks.explanation: Graded on the prediction canvas against the reference curve.

checks.prompt: Explain in one sentence what the cut-in voltage is.
checks.answer: The cut-in voltage is the forward voltage, about 0.7 V for silicon, above which the diode current increases rapidly.
checks.explanation: Include the value and the word 'rapidly' or 'sharply'.

concepts.title: Diode models
concepts.canDo: Choose a diode model and calculate the current in a simple circuit.

misconceptions.statement: A diode has 0.7 V across it even when reverse biased.
misconceptions.correction: In reverse bias it is almost an open circuit; the 0.7 V applies only when it conducts.

misconceptions.statement: The ideal model is fine for any circuit.
misconceptions.correction: For supplies of a few volts, the 0.7 V drop matters; use the constant-voltage-drop model.

explanation.keyIdea: Use the simplest model that is accurate enough: ideal for large supplies, a 0.7 V drop for small ones.
explanation.text: A diode model replaces the real curve with something simple enough to calculate with. In the ideal diode model, a forward-biased diode is a short circuit and a reverse-biased diode is an open circuit. In the constant-voltage-drop model, a conducting silicon diode has a fixed 0.7 V across it. The piecewise-linear model adds a small forward resistance in series with that 0.7 V. Choose the simplest model that is accurate enough: when the supply is much larger than 0.7 V, the ideal model is close; for small supplies, use the constant-voltage-drop model.

visual.description: Three equivalent circuits side by side: ideal (a closed switch), constant drop (switch plus a 0.7 V cell), piecewise linear (switch, 0.7 V cell and a small resistor rf).
visual.alt: Ideal, constant-voltage-drop and piecewise-linear diode models

walkthrough.say: In the ideal diode model, a conducting diode is just a short circuit.
The constant-voltage-drop model keeps 0.7 V across a conducting silicon diode.
The piecewise-linear model adds a small forward resistance.
Choose the simplest model that is accurate enough for your supply.

example.title: 5 V, 1 kΩ and a silicon diode
example.scenario: A silicon diode and a 1 kΩ resistor are in series across 5 V, forward biased. Ideal model: I = 5/1000 = 5 mA. Constant-voltage-drop model: I = (5 − 0.7)/1000 = 4.3 mA. Piecewise-linear with rf = 20 Ω: I = 4.3/1020 ≈ 4.22 mA.
example.takeaway: The models differ by about 15% here because 5 V is not much larger than 0.7 V.

workedQuestion.prompt: A silicon diode is connected in series with a 2.2 kΩ resistor across a 12 V supply in forward bias. Find the current using (a) the ideal model and (b) the constant-voltage-drop model. Which is closer to the real value, and why?
modelAnswer: (a) Ideal model: the diode is a short circuit, so I = 12 V / 2.2 kΩ = 5.45 mA.
(b) Constant-voltage-drop model: I = (12 − 0.7) V / 2.2 kΩ = 11.3 / 2200 = 5.14 mA.
The constant-voltage-drop model is closer, because a real silicon diode has about 0.7 V across it while conducting.
The difference is small (about 6%) because 12 V is much larger than 0.7 V.

rubric.criterion: Chooses the closer model with a reason

checks.prompt: A silicon diode and a 1 kΩ resistor are in series across 5 V, forward biased. Using the constant-voltage-drop model, find the current.
checks.answer: 4.3 mA

checks.prompt: In the ideal model, a forward-biased diode behaves like:
checks.answer: A short circuit
checks.explanation: Ideal: short when forward, open when reverse.

checks.prompt: Match the term: forward resistance
options: The small resistance of a conducting diode
checks.answer: The small resistance of a conducting diode
checks.explanation: It is added in series in the piecewise-linear model.

checks.prompt: When is the ideal diode model good enough?
checks.answer: When the supply voltage is much larger than the 0.7 V diode drop.
checks.explanation: Then the 0.7 V is a small fraction of the total.

concepts.title: Half-wave rectifier
concepts.canDo: Explain how a half-wave rectifier turns AC into pulsating DC and sketch its waveforms.

misconceptions.statement: The negative half is flipped upwards at the output.
misconceptions.correction: That is a full-wave rectifier; a half-wave rectifier simply removes the negative half.

misconceptions.statement: Turning the diode round makes no difference.
misconceptions.correction: A reversed diode passes only the negative half-cycles.

explanation.keyIdea: One diode passes only the positive half-cycles, so the output is pulsating DC with an average of Vm/π.
explanation.text: A rectifier converts AC into DC. In a half-wave rectifier, one diode is placed in series with the load. During the positive half-cycle of the input, the diode is forward biased and conducts, so that half-cycle appears across the load. During the negative half-cycle, the diode is reverse biased and blocks, so the output is zero. The output is pulsating DC: positive half-cycles separated by gaps, at the same frequency as the input. Its average value is Vm/π, about 0.318 Vm.

visual.description: Transformer secondary, one diode and load resistor RL; the input sine wave above and the output with only positive half-cycles below, on the same time axis.
visual.alt: Half-wave rectifier circuit with input sine and output of positive half-cycles

walkthrough.say: A rectifier converts AC into DC.
In the positive half-cycle the diode is forward biased and conducts.
In the negative half it blocks. Exam words: conducts, then blocks.
The result is pulsating DC: one direction, but in bumps.

beats: The input sine wave arrives
Positive half: current flows through the diode to the load
Negative half: the diode blocks, the output is flat
Only the bumps remain: pulsating DC

interactive.prompt: Run the half-wave rectifier and look at the output.

example.title: The rectifier lab
example.scenario: A 230 V to 12 V (RMS) transformer feeds a 1N4007 diode and a 1 kΩ load. The peak is Vm = 12 × √2 ≈ 17 V. After the 0.7 V drop the output peak is about 16.3 V, and the average is 16.3/π ≈ 5.2 V.
example.takeaway: Half the waveform is thrown away, so the average output is low.

workedQuestion.prompt: Explain the working of a half-wave rectifier with a neat circuit diagram and waveforms.
modelAnswer: A half-wave rectifier converts AC into pulsating DC using a single diode in series with the load resistor RL.
During the positive half-cycle, the diode is forward biased and conducts, so current flows through RL and the output follows the input.
During the negative half-cycle, the diode is reverse biased and blocks current, so the output voltage is zero.
The output therefore has only the positive half-cycles, at the same frequency as the input. The average output is Vdc = Vm/π.
(Diagram: transformer, diode and RL; input sine wave and output with only positive half-cycles.)

checks.prompt: For a 50 Hz input, the output frequency of a half-wave rectifier is:
checks.answer: 50 Hz
checks.explanation: There is one output pulse per input cycle.

checks.prompt: An ideal half-wave rectifier has a peak input of 20 V. Find the average output voltage.
checks.explanation: Vdc = Vm/π = 20/π = 6.37 V.

checks.prompt: Match the term: pulsating DC
options: Current in one direction that rises and falls in pulses
checks.answer: Current in one direction that rises and falls in pulses
checks.explanation: It is DC because it never reverses, but it is not steady.

checks.prompt: Why is the negative half-cycle missing at the output?
checks.answer: During the negative half-cycle the diode is reverse biased, so it blocks current and the output is zero.
checks.explanation: Use 'reverse biased' and 'blocks'.

checks.prompt: Before you run the simulation, sketch the output across RL.
checks.answer: Positive half-cycles only, flat at zero during the negative halves.
checks.explanation: Compared on the prediction canvas with the simulated output.

concepts.title: Centre-tap full-wave rectifier
concepts.canDo: Explain how a centre-tap rectifier uses both halves of the AC cycle.

misconceptions.statement: Both diodes conduct at the same time.
misconceptions.correction: They take turns: D1 in the positive half-cycle, D2 in the negative half-cycle.

explanation.keyIdea: Two diodes take turns, so both halves reach the load in the same direction: average 2Vm/π, ripple at twice the mains frequency.
explanation.text: A centre-tap full-wave rectifier uses a transformer with a centre-tapped secondary and two diodes. During the positive half-cycle, the top half of the secondary forward biases D1, which conducts. During the negative half-cycle, the bottom half forward biases D2. Both diodes send current through the load in the same direction, so both half-cycles appear at the output. The output repeats at twice the input frequency, the average is 2Vm/π, where Vm is the peak of each half of the secondary, and each diode must withstand a peak inverse voltage of 2Vm.

visual.description: Centre-tapped transformer, D1 on the top end and D2 on the bottom end joined at the load RL, return to the centre tap. Current paths for each half-cycle in two colours; input and full-wave output waveforms.
visual.alt: Centre-tap full-wave rectifier with current paths for both half-cycles

walkthrough.say: The transformer has a centre-tapped secondary: a connection in the middle.
Both diodes push current through the load in the same direction.
So the output bumps come at twice the input frequency.
Exam phrase: peak inverse voltage, 2Vm for the centre-tap rectifier.

example.title: Same mains, twice the bumps
example.scenario: With each half of the secondary giving Vm = 15 V, an ideal centre-tap rectifier gives Vdc = 2 × 15/π ≈ 9.55 V, and on 50 Hz mains the output repeats 100 times a second.
example.takeaway: Using both halves doubles the average and the ripple frequency.

workedQuestion.prompt: Explain the working of a centre-tap full-wave rectifier with a circuit diagram and waveforms. State the PIV of each diode.
modelAnswer: The circuit uses a centre-tapped transformer and two diodes, D1 and D2, connected to the load RL.
During the positive half-cycle, D1 is forward biased and conducts, while D2 is reverse biased; current flows through RL.
During the negative half-cycle, D2 is forward biased and conducts, while D1 is reverse biased; current flows through RL in the same direction.
The output therefore contains both half-cycles, at twice the input frequency, with Vdc = 2Vm/π.
When a diode is reverse biased it sees the full secondary voltage, so the PIV of each diode is 2Vm.

rubric.criterion: Circuit with centre-tapped transformer and two diodes

checks.prompt: On 50 Hz mains, the output of a full-wave rectifier repeats at:
checks.answer: 100 Hz
checks.explanation: Two output pulses per input cycle.

checks.prompt: Each half of the secondary has a peak of 15 V. Find the average output of an ideal centre-tap rectifier.
Match the term: centre-tap transformer
options: A transformer whose secondary has a connection at its midpoint
checks.answer: A transformer whose secondary has a connection at its midpoint
checks.explanation: The midpoint is the return for both halves.

checks.prompt: Why must each diode in a centre-tap rectifier withstand 2Vm?
checks.answer: When one diode conducts, the reverse-biased diode sees the full secondary voltage, which peaks at 2Vm.
checks.explanation: Use 'reverse biased' and 'full secondary voltage'.

concepts.title: Bridge rectifier
concepts.canDo: Explain how a bridge rectifier works and compare it with the centre-tap rectifier.

misconceptions.statement: All four diodes conduct at once.
misconceptions.correction: Two opposite diodes conduct in each half-cycle.

misconceptions.statement: One diode the wrong way round in the bridge doesn't matter.
misconceptions.correction: A reversed diode stops rectification or shorts the supply in one half-cycle.

explanation.keyIdea: Four diodes give full-wave output without a centre tap, with two diode drops and a PIV of only Vm.
explanation.text: A bridge rectifier uses four diodes and needs no centre tap. During the positive half-cycle, two opposite diodes conduct; during the negative half-cycle, the other two conduct. In both half-cycles, current flows through the load in the same direction, so the output is full-wave. Because two diodes are always in the current path, the output peak is Vm − 1.4 V for silicon diodes. Each diode's peak inverse voltage is only Vm, and the whole transformer secondary is used in both half-cycles.

visual.description: Four diodes in a diamond, AC input on the left and right corners, load RL across the top and bottom corners; the conducting pair highlighted for each half-cycle.
visual.alt: Bridge rectifier with the conducting diode pair for each half-cycle

walkthrough.say: A bridge rectifier uses four diodes.
Exam phrase: a bridge needs no centre tap.
In each half-cycle, two opposite diodes conduct.

walkthrough.target: two diodes are always in the current path
walkthrough.say: Two diodes are always in the path, so you lose about 1.4 V.

example.title: The input of a mains adapter
example.scenario: Most mains adapters start with a bridge of four diodes, often in one small package, because it gives full-wave output from an ordinary transformer, or directly from the mains.
example.takeaway: A bridge gives full-wave output without a centre tap, at the cost of two diode drops.

workedQuestion.prompt: Compare the centre-tap and bridge full-wave rectifiers.
modelAnswer: Number of diodes: the centre-tap rectifier uses two; the bridge uses four.
Transformer: the centre-tap rectifier needs a centre-tapped transformer; the bridge needs no centre tap.
Peak inverse voltage: 2Vm for each diode in the centre-tap rectifier; only Vm in the bridge.
Diode drops: one diode conducts at a time in the centre-tap rectifier (output peak Vm − 0.7 V); two in the bridge (Vm − 1.4 V).
Transformer use: each half of a centre-tap secondary works for only half the cycle; the whole bridge secondary works in both halves, so the transformer can be smaller.

checks.prompt: In a bridge rectifier, how many diodes conduct at any instant?
checks.explanation: One opposite pair per half-cycle.

checks.prompt: A bridge rectifier with silicon diodes (constant-voltage-drop model) has Vm = 12 V. Find the average output voltage.
Match the term: bridge rectifier
options: A full-wave rectifier of four diodes that needs no centre tap
A half-wave rectifier with two diodes
A filter made of four capacitors
checks.answer: A full-wave rectifier of four diodes that needs no centre tap
checks.explanation: Four diodes in a diamond.

checks.prompt: Give one advantage of a bridge rectifier over a centre-tap rectifier.
checks.answer: It needs no centre-tapped transformer, and each diode only has to withstand Vm.
checks.explanation: Either advantage earns the mark; write it as a full sentence.

concepts.title: Rectifier figures of merit
concepts.canDo: Calculate and compare the ripple factor, efficiency and PIV of rectifiers.

misconceptions.statement: A higher ripple factor is better.
misconceptions.correction: A lower ripple factor means smoother DC.

misconceptions.statement: PIV is the same for every rectifier.
misconceptions.correction: Vm for half-wave and bridge, 2Vm for centre-tap.

explanation.keyIdea: Ripple factor, efficiency and PIV turn 'which rectifier is better' into numbers; full-wave wins on ripple and efficiency.
explanation.text: Figures of merit let us compare rectifiers with numbers. The average (DC) value is what a DC meter reads; the RMS value includes the AC part as well. The ripple factor is the RMS value of the AC component divided by the DC value: γ = √((Vrms/Vdc)² − 1). It is 1.21 for a half-wave rectifier and 0.482 for a full-wave rectifier, so full-wave output is much smoother. Rectification efficiency is DC output power divided by AC input power, at most 40.6% for half-wave and 81.2% for full-wave. The peak inverse voltage (PIV) is the largest reverse voltage a diode must withstand: Vm for half-wave and bridge, 2Vm for centre-tap.

visual.description: A comparison card of three columns (half-wave, centre-tap, bridge) with rows for Vdc, ripple factor, maximum efficiency and PIV.
visual.alt: Table comparing rectifier figures of merit

walkthrough.say: The ripple factor measures how much AC is left on the DC.

walkthrough.target: 1.21 for a half-wave rectifier and 0.482 for a full-wave rectifier
walkthrough.say: Half-wave 1.21, full-wave 0.482: full-wave is much smoother.
Rectification efficiency is DC power out over AC power in.
PIV is the largest reverse voltage a diode must survive.

example.title: Choosing a rectifier for a charger
example.scenario: A designer compares the options: half-wave gives γ = 1.21 and at most 40.6% efficiency; full-wave gives γ = 0.482 and up to 81.2%. Full-wave wins on both, so it is used almost everywhere.
example.takeaway: Figures of merit make the choice obvious and defensible.

workedQuestion.prompt: Define ripple factor and derive its value for a half-wave rectifier.
modelAnswer: Ripple factor γ = (RMS value of the AC component of the output) / (DC value of the output).
Since Vrms² = Vdc² + Vac², γ = √((Vrms/Vdc)² − 1).
For a half-wave rectifier, Vdc = Vm/π and Vrms = Vm/2.
So Vrms/Vdc = (Vm/2)/(Vm/π) = π/2 = 1.571.

checks.explanation: Bridge PIV = Vm. In practice, pick a rating with margin, such as 50 V.

concepts.title: How a capacitor filter smooths
concepts.canDo: Explain how a capacitor filter smooths the output of a rectifier.

misconceptions.statement: The capacitor removes all the AC, giving perfect DC.
misconceptions.correction: A small ripple always remains; a bigger capacitor only reduces it.

misconceptions.statement: The capacitor can go in series with the load.
misconceptions.correction: In series it blocks DC entirely; it must be across the load.

explanation.keyIdea: The capacitor charges to the peak, then discharges slowly through the load to fill the gaps.
explanation.text: The output of a rectifier still pulses. A capacitor filter is a large capacitor connected across the load. While the rectified voltage rises towards its peak, the diode conducts and the capacitor charges to the peak. When the input falls below the capacitor voltage, the diode stops conducting and the capacitor discharges slowly through the load, filling the gap until the next peak. The output becomes a nearly steady DC with a small sawtooth-shaped ripple. A larger capacitor or a larger load resistance makes the discharge slower and the ripple smaller.

visual.description: Rectified output dashed; filtered output solid, rising to each peak and sloping down gently until the next peak; charge and discharge segments labelled.
visual.alt: Capacitor-filtered output: charging to the peak, slow discharge, small sawtooth ripple

walkthrough.say: A capacitor filter is a big capacitor across the load.
While the voltage rises, the capacitor charges to the peak.
Then it discharges slowly through the load, filling the gap.
What is left is a small ripple.

beats: Bumpy rectified output
The capacitor fills up at each peak
Between peaks it drains slowly into the load
The result: nearly flat DC with a small ripple

example.title: A tank under a tap that runs in bursts
example.scenario: A tap that gushes and stops (the rectifier) fills a tank (the capacitor). The pipe out of the tank (the load) keeps flowing steadily, even between gushes. A bigger tank gives a steadier flow.
example.takeaway: The capacitor stores charge at the peaks and releases it in the gaps.

workedQuestion.prompt: Why is a capacitor filter used after a rectifier? Explain how it smooths the output, with waveforms.
modelAnswer: The output of a rectifier is pulsating DC, which is not suitable for electronic circuits, so a capacitor filter is used to smooth it.
A large capacitor is connected across the load. While the rectified voltage rises, the diode conducts and the capacitor charges to the peak value.
When the input falls below the capacitor voltage, the diode is reverse biased and stops conducting; the capacitor then discharges slowly through the load.
The output therefore stays close to the peak, with a small sawtooth ripple. (Waveform: rectified output and the smoothed output.)
A larger capacitance or larger load resistance slows the discharge and reduces the ripple.

rubric.criterion: Effect of C and RL on ripple

checks.prompt: Increasing the filter capacitance:

checks.explanation: A bigger capacitor discharges more slowly.

checks.explanation: Ripple is what the filter tries to reduce.

checks.prompt: What does the capacitor do when the diode stops conducting?
checks.answer: It discharges through the load and keeps the output voltage up until the next peak.
checks.explanation: Use 'discharges' and 'through the load'.

concepts.title: Ripple voltage and choosing the capacitor
concepts.canDo: Estimate the ripple of a capacitor filter and choose a capacitor for a ripple target.

misconceptions.statement: Ripple depends only on the capacitance.
misconceptions.correction: It also depends on the load current and the mains frequency.

misconceptions.statement: The full-wave formula uses f, not 2f.
misconceptions.correction: Full-wave recharges twice per cycle, so use 2f.

explanation.keyIdea: Ripple ≈ load current ÷ (refill rate × C); full-wave refills twice as often, so it needs half the capacitance.
explanation.text: We can estimate how big the ripple is. For a capacitor filter, the peak-to-peak ripple voltage is approximately Vr = Idc / (f·C) for a half-wave rectifier and Vr = Idc / (2f·C) for a full-wave rectifier, where Idc is the load current and f is the mains frequency. Full-wave refills the capacitor twice as often, so it needs half the capacitance for the same ripple. To choose a capacitor, rearrange: C = Idc / (2f·Vr) for full-wave, then pick the next larger standard value.

visual.description: Filtered full-wave output with the peak-to-peak ripple Vr marked between the highest and lowest points, and the discharge time between refills marked.
visual.alt: Peak-to-peak ripple voltage on a filtered full-wave output

walkthrough.say: The peak-to-peak ripple voltage is the gap between the highest and lowest output.
For full-wave, Vr is the load current over two f times C.
Full-wave refills twice as often, so it needs half the capacitance.
Exam move: rearrange the formula to find C.

interactive.prompt: Change the load current and the capacitor. How big is the ripple?

example.title: A supply for a microcontroller
example.scenario: A full-wave rectifier on 50 Hz mains supplies 100 mA through a 1000 µF capacitor: Vr = 0.1 / (2 × 50 × 0.001) = 1 V peak-to-peak.
example.takeaway: Using 2200 µF instead would cut the ripple to about 0.45 V.

workedQuestion.prompt: A full-wave rectifier on 50 Hz mains supplies 200 mA to a load. Find the filter capacitance needed to keep the peak-to-peak ripple at or below 1 V, and choose a standard value.
modelAnswer: For a full-wave rectifier with a capacitor filter, Vr ≈ Idc / (2f·C).
Rearranging: C = Idc / (2f·Vr).
Choose the next larger standard value: 2200 µF.
Check: with 2200 µF, Vr = 0.2 / (100 × 0.0022) ≈ 0.91 V, which meets the 1 V limit.

checks.answer: half
checks.explanation: It refills the capacitor twice per mains cycle.

checks.answer: The difference between the highest and lowest output voltage
checks.explanation: Vr is measured from top to bottom of the ripple.

checks.explanation: Use 'recharges' and 'twice per cycle'.

concepts.title: The Zener diode and breakdown
concepts.canDo: Explain Zener and avalanche breakdown and why a Zener diode holds a steady voltage.

misconceptions.statement: Breakdown always destroys a diode.
misconceptions.correction: A Zener diode is designed to operate in breakdown safely, within its power rating.

misconceptions.statement: A Zener regulates in forward bias.
misconceptions.correction: It regulates in reverse breakdown; forward biased it just drops about 0.7 V.

explanation.keyIdea: A Zener diode works in reverse breakdown, where its voltage stays nearly constant over a wide range of current.
explanation.text: A Zener diode is a heavily doped diode designed to work in reverse breakdown without damage. In forward bias it behaves like an ordinary diode. In reverse bias, once the voltage reaches the Zener voltage Vz, the current rises sharply while the voltage across it stays nearly constant. Below about 5 V, breakdown is mainly Zener breakdown: the strong field across the very thin depletion region pulls electrons directly out of their bonds. Above about 6 V, it is mainly avalanche breakdown: fast carriers knock out more carriers in a chain reaction.

visual.description: Zener V-I curve: normal forward branch; reverse branch flat until −Vz, then a near-vertical line labelled Vz; Zener symbol beside it.
visual.alt: Zener diode characteristic with the near-vertical breakdown at Vz

walkthrough.say: A Zener diode is built to work in reverse breakdown.
Its breakdown point is the Zener voltage, Vz.
The key idea: the voltage stays nearly constant as current changes.
At higher voltages, the mechanism is avalanche breakdown.

example.title: A 5.1 V reference
example.scenario: A 5.1 V Zener diode, reverse biased through a resistor, keeps about 5.1 V across it whether its current is 5 mA or 30 mA.
example.takeaway: A Zener diode is a voltage holder, not a one-way gate.

workedQuestion.prompt: Explain Zener breakdown and avalanche breakdown. How are they different?
modelAnswer: Zener breakdown occurs in heavily doped junctions with a very thin depletion region. At a low reverse voltage (below about 5 V), the strong electric field pulls electrons directly out of their covalent bonds, so the reverse current rises sharply.

Avalanche breakdown occurs in lightly doped junctions at higher reverse voltages (above about 6 V). Minority carriers gain enough energy to knock electrons out of bonds when they collide, and those carriers knock out more, in a chain reaction.
Differences: Zener breakdown happens at low voltage in heavily doped diodes; avalanche happens at higher voltage in lightly doped diodes.
The Zener breakdown voltage falls slightly as temperature rises (negative temperature coefficient); the avalanche voltage rises with temperature (positive temperature coefficient).

rubric.criterion: At least one clear difference (doping, voltage or temperature coefficient)

checks.prompt: A Zener diode used as a regulator is operated in:
checks.answer: Reverse breakdown
checks.explanation: That is where its voltage stays nearly constant.

checks.prompt: Breakdown in a 3.3 V Zener diode is mainly:
checks.answer: Zener breakdown
checks.explanation: Below about 5 V, the Zener mechanism dominates.

checks.prompt: Match the term: Zener voltage
options: The reverse voltage at which a Zener diode breaks down and holds steady
The forward voltage of an LED
The peak of the AC input
checks.answer: The reverse voltage at which a Zener diode breaks down and holds steady
checks.explanation: Written Vz.

checks.prompt: How is avalanche breakdown different from Zener breakdown?
checks.answer: Avalanche breakdown happens at higher voltages when fast carriers knock out more carriers, while Zener breakdown happens at low voltages when a strong field pulls electrons out of their bonds.
checks.explanation: Compare both the voltage and the mechanism.

concepts.title: The Zener voltage regulator
concepts.canDo: Design a Zener regulator and explain how it holds the output constant.

misconceptions.statement: The series resistor isn't needed.
misconceptions.correction: Without Rs the Zener current is unlimited and the diode burns out.

misconceptions.statement: The Zener goes in series with the load.
misconceptions.correction: It goes in parallel with the load, with Rs in series.

explanation.keyIdea: Rs sets the total current; the Zener in parallel takes whatever the load doesn't, so the load voltage stays at Vz.
explanation.text: A Zener voltage regulator holds the load voltage constant even when the input or the load changes. The Zener diode is connected in reverse bias, in parallel with the load, and a series resistor Rs drops the difference between the input and the Zener voltage. The current through Rs is I = (Vin − Vz)/Rs, and it splits between the Zener and the load: I = Iz + IL. If the input rises, the extra current flows into the Zener and the output stays at Vz. If the load draws more, the Zener takes less. This ability to hold the output as the load changes is called load regulation. Rs must keep Iz above its minimum at full load, and the Zener power Vz × Iz must stay within its rating at no load.

visual.description: Unregulated input, series resistor Rs, Zener diode (reverse biased) in parallel with load RL; current arrows I, Iz and IL; Vout = Vz marked.
visual.alt: Zener voltage regulator with series resistor and load

walkthrough.say: The series resistor Rs drops the extra voltage.
The Zener sits in parallel with the load, holding it at Vz.
The current through Rs splits: I equals Iz plus IL.
Exam phrase: load regulation.

example.title: 5.1 V for a microcontroller from 12 V
example.scenario: Vin = 12 V, Vz = 5.1 V, IL = 20 mA and a minimum Iz of 10 mA: Rs = (12 − 5.1)/0.030 = 230 Ω, so use 220 Ω. Then I = 6.9/220 ≈ 31 mA.
example.takeaway: Rs sets the total current; the Zener soaks up whatever the load doesn't take.

workedQuestion.prompt: Design a Zener regulator to supply 5.1 V to a 20 mA load from a 12 V input, keeping at least 10 mA in the Zener. Find Rs, choose a standard value, and find the Zener power at no load.
modelAnswer: Total current at full load: I = Iz(min) + IL = 10 mA + 20 mA = 30 mA.
Choose the next lower standard value, 220 Ω, so that Iz stays above 10 mA: I = 6.9/220 = 31.4 mA, giving Iz = 11.4 mA at full load.
At no load, all 31.4 mA flows through the Zener: Pz = Vz × Iz = 5.1 × 0.0314 = 0.16 W.
Use a Zener rated 0.5 W for a safe margin.

checks.prompt: Vin = 10 V, Vz = 6.2 V, Rs = 100 Ω and IL = 20 mA. Find the Zener current.
checks.answer: 18 mA

checks.explanation: The total through Rs is fixed by Vin and Vz, so the Zener gives up current to the load.

checks.explanation: Use 'extra current', 'flows into the Zener' and 'stays at Vz'.
